items.title: There are true statements about numbers that cannot be proved
items.claim: Hilbert (1900) hoped to put mathematics on a complete, consistent axiomatic foundation. In 1931, Kurt Gödel proved it impossible. Any system of axioms expressive enough to do basic arithmetic contains true statements that the system cannot prove.
items.prompt: What's the heart of Gödel's argument?

options.text: Gödel constructed a self-referential statement G: 'G cannot be proved within this system'. If the system could prove G, the system would prove something false (contradiction). If the system can't prove G, then G is true and unprovable

items.reveal:
Gödel encoded statements about mathematics AS numbers (Gödel numbering), so the system could 'talk about itself'. He then constructed a sentence asserting its own unprovability.

First incompleteness theorem: any consistent system strong enough to express arithmetic contains a true statement it cannot prove.
Second incompleteness theorem: such a system cannot prove its own consistency from within itself.

The results devastated Hilbert's program. They also bounded what computers can do: the halting problem (Turing 1936) is undecidable in essentially the same way.

Gödel was 25 when he proved it. Hilbert took it badly. Gödel later starved himself to death (1978) — convinced his food was being poisoned, he stopped eating when his wife was hospitalised.

Mathematics is still consistent (presumably), still useful, still extending — just provably incomplete.
items.why: Mathematics is treated as a closed, fully derivable system. Gödel showed any rich enough system has fundamental gaps — true things it can never prove.

items.title: The most important open problem in mathematics
items.claim: Riemann conjectured in 1859 that all non-trivial zeros of the zeta function lie on the line Re(s) = 1/2. The conjecture controls the distribution of primes among integers. Proving (or disproving) it has been unsolved for 165 years.
items.prompt: Why do we care about complex zeros of a strange function?

options.text: The distribution of prime numbers is encoded in the zeros of the Riemann zeta function — proving the Riemann hypothesis would establish a vast number of theorems in number theory that are currently conditional on it
It tells us the value of zeta at integer points
It's part of the definition of pi

items.reveal:
Riemann's only paper on number theory (1859) defined the analytic continuation of the zeta function and noted that the function has 'trivial zeros' at -2, -4, -6, ... and other 'non-trivial zeros' in the strip 0 less than Re(s) less than 1. He conjectured all non-trivial zeros lie exactly on Re(s) = 1/2.

The Prime Number Theorem (Hadamard, de la Vallée Poussin, 1896) says the count of primes up to x is asymptotically x / ln x. The Riemann hypothesis would tighten the error term enormously.

Thousands of theorems in modern number theory are stated 'assuming RH'. A proof would make them unconditional. Conversely, a disproof would force major rewrites.

The first 10 trillion non-trivial zeros have all been computed and verified to lie on Re(s) = 1/2 (Gourdon, 2004). This doesn't prove the hypothesis.

The Clay Mathematics Institute lists it as one of seven Millennium Prize Problems, with a $1,000,000 reward. So far, only Poincaré (Perelman, 2003) has been solved.
items.why: Primes look like a chaotic distribution. The Riemann hypothesis says they have hidden, beautiful regularity controlled by complex analysis — and 165 years of effort haven't proved or disproved it.

items.title: If a stock falls 50% then rises 50%, you've LOST money
items.claim: Stock at 100. Falls 50%: now 50. Rises 50%: now 75. Two equal-percentage moves in opposite directions don't cancel.

options.text: Percentages are RATIOS, not amounts. The 50% drop reduces the base; the subsequent 50% rise is on a smaller base. To recover from a -50% loss you need a +100% gain

items.reveal:
To go from x to y, percentage change is (y - x) / x.

Loss of L percent: new value = old * (1 - L/100).
Gain of G percent: new value = old * (1 + G/100).

For symmetric percent moves NOT to cancel, multiply: (1 - 0.5)(1 + 0.5) = 0.75. Always less than 1 if the magnitude is the same.

Recovery table:
- Lose 10%: need 11.1% to recover.
- Lose 25%: need 33.3% to recover.
- Lose 50%: need 100% to recover.
- Lose 75%: need 300% to recover.
- Lose 90%: need 900% to recover.

Applications:
- Drawdowns in investing: deep losses require enormous gains to recover. A 50% bear market loss takes years of strong returns to break even.
- Discounted prices then surcharged: 50% off followed by 50% on actually leaves you at 75% of original price (consumer gets a deal).
- Inflation: 10% inflation for 7 years halves purchasing power, even though 70% < 100%.

Geometric vs arithmetic mean: a stock returning +50%, -50%, +50%, -50% has arithmetic mean return 0% but geometric (actual) mean of ((1.5 * 0.5 * 1.5 * 0.5)^0.25 - 1) = -13.4%/period.
items.why: Percentages feel symmetric. They're multiplicative ratios that don't cancel directly. Anyone interpreting investment returns, weight changes, price comparisons or compound growth without realising this misreads the data.
